items.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996
items.q: The younger guys can play everything. They’re into James Brown.

ctx.x: Well, I think we have to stop categorizing. Like now you know I’m doing this electric thing, and because I grew up doing it. But also I play jazz. And so you’re going to hear my things be a little bit more aggressive than what they call that soft jazz. Because we’re still up there really trying to mesh and play. But that’s not all I do. Like I mentioned earlier, I play in the church so I’d like to do a Gospel record at some point. And here’s another thing I see that really has changed the dynamics of the music.…

play. They can really play. You can not say that jazz is American anymore. Jazz started in America, particularly by black people. But now it has spread throughout the world and has become a proven formula. And it’s transcended all racial, sexual and religious nationalistic lines, that if you submit to the music, you will have success, and be able to get to what you’re saying inside. Because now there are young kids from other countries that understand what this music is about. So now, when me and my generations…

people. But my problem is all these young people that were young in 1959, it’s 1995 they’re coming to my gigs and wanting me to do 1959. Where are the young people? I want the young people. That’s what I learned from Art. You’ve got to have the young people there. And once you know you’re tapped into the young folks, you know you’re on the right track. So this is the thing I see for the future of the music is that we have an obligation to sit in and deal with the rap, deal with the DJs, deal with all of that…
